players.product: trapped-ion quantum computers (Forte, Forte Enterprise) sold as systems and as cloud access, plus quantum networking, sensing and security products

quarterly_data.signal: IonQ Q2 2026 revenue was $80.1 million, up 287% year-on-year - the strongest quarter in its history and the fifth consecutive record quarter. CFO: revenue exceeded the company's own expectations by 20%; the largest driver of the outperformance was the continued deployment of fifth-generation quantum computing systems.
quarterly_data.figure: $80.1 million revenue; 287% year-on-year growth; 20% above own expectations

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: Q2 organic revenue grew 132% year-over-year on global quantum computer deployments; for the full year IonQ still expects organic revenue to grow approximately 100%, as guided at the start of the year. This year Tempo quantum computing revenue is the principal driver; next year the company expects its semiconductor-based (electronic qubit control) computers to become the main driver.
quarterly_data.figure: organic revenue +132% year-over-year in Q2; FY2026 organic growth expected approximately 100%

quarterly_data.signal: IonQ raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $280 million-$290 million; the range covers IonQ only (SkyWater operated as a separate public company through Q2). CFO: combined-company revenue and EBITDA guidance will come after integration, once intercompany revenue eliminations and purchase-price accounting are worked through; management says it does not plan for a quarterly revenue decline in the second half.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue guidance $280 million-$290 million (IonQ only, raised)

quarterly_data.signal: IonQ ended Q2 with $485 million in remaining performance obligations, up from $470 million in Q1 and $122 million a year earlier; CFO: RPO was replenished after being drawn down into revenue in a record quarter. CFO: no dollars from the Anduril and Sandia MOU relationships (as named in the question) are included in RPO; CEO: the MOUs are not yet in the company's numbers because they are still at an early stage.

CFO revenue metrics for Q2 (given as color, may vary by quarter): approximately 50% of revenue came from international customers (countries including Australia, South Korea, Portugal, India, Denmark, Germany, Israel, Japan), helped by the KISTI and QuantumBasel deployments; 60% came from commercial (non-U.S. government) customers; multi-product sales grew 40% year-over-year and are about 25% of revenue. IonQ delivers solutions in over 50 countries.
quarterly_data.figure: ~50% international; 60% commercial; multi-product sales +40% year-over-year, ~25% of revenue; over 50 countries

quarterly_data.signal: Customer KISTI: in Q2 IonQ began shipping subsystems of its fifth-generation quantum computing system to the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI); the system is being delivered and assembled at the customer site in Korea.

Customer QuantumBasel (Switzerland): IonQ's fifth-generation machine is in final assembly on site next to the fourth-generation machine QuantumBasel previously purchased from IonQ; CFO believes it is the world's first deployment of two consecutive quantum computer generations side by side in a commercial setting.

Q2 costs: GAAP operating expenses $417.3 million ($201.2 million non-GAAP), of which R&D $160.6 million; adjusted EBITDA was $-120.3 million, including about $20 million of higher spending with SkyWater (roadmap acceleration) and about $10 million of pre-integration and supply-chain costs ahead of the SkyWater close. GAAP net loss was $-1.9 billion, mainly a roughly $1.6 billion non-cash warrant mark-to-market charge.
quarterly_data.figure: GAAP opex $417.3 million; non-GAAP opex $201.2 million; R&D $160.6 million; adjusted EBITDA $-120.3 million; GAAP net loss $-1.9 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Supplier SkyWater Technology: CFO estimates IonQ's full-year 2026 spending with SkyWater under their commercial agreement at approximately $120 million (higher than forecast at the start of the year, as the roadmap work is succeeding); CFO: 'I think we're their biggest customer already.' After the acquisition closed, this intercompany revenue will be eliminated on consolidation.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately $120 million FY2026 spending with SkyWater

quarterly_data.signal: Electronic-qubit-control chip roadmap: three tape-outs announced in February 2026, first chip prototypes received in May 2026, and in Q2 IonQ received its first fully featured, fully integrated QPUs from SkyWater, now in testing at College Park. CEO: IonQ plans to begin commissioning 256-qubit systems in 2027 - commissioning, deploying and spooling up the manufacturing line in the first half of next year 'remains all on track'; it is working on at least three chip generations in parallel, the 10,000-qubit chip is beginning to be taped out, and it is accelerating its path to 10,000 qubits in 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: 256-qubit systems commissioning in first half of 2027; 10,000 qubits targeted in 2027

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: fifth-generation machines are being deployed now, the sixth generation is to be deployed next year and the seventh the year after, with fault-tolerant computing delivered within that roadmap; customers are asking to buy Tempo now and be first in line for the 256-qubit or 10,000-qubit machine.

CEO: in April IonQ released its 'walking cat' architecture, which it calls the industry's first end-to-end manufacturable blueprint of a fault-tolerant quantum computer; in Q2 it demonstrated breakeven quantum error correction using QLDPC codes on a test system, validating key elements of that architecture. In October of the prior year it reported 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity without ground-state cooling.

CEO: SkyWater (acquisition closed the week before the call) makes IonQ what it calls the only vertically integrated, full-stack quantum platform, owning design, fabrication, packaging and deployment in U.S. facilities. IonQ will keep SkyWater as a merchant quantum foundry serving all modalities (superconducting, photonics, ions, atoms) with IP protection; CEO calls SkyWater the only quantum foundry operating today, at a 200 mm price point he expects to stay compelling. CFO: vertical integration is expected to lower IonQ's quantum hardware development costs over time.

In Q2 IonQ acquired UC Santa Barbara spinoff Nexus Photonics (chip-scale integration of lasers, modulators and optical subsystems); it has begun integrating the technology into its next-generation atomic clocks and gravimeters and plans to supply these integrated components to the quantum ecosystem through a dedicated quantum photonics foundry offering at SkyWater. CEO: IonQ already sold atomic clocks, sensors and networking products to other quantum companies before the SkyWater deal and calls itself the world's largest quantum merchant supplier.

In Q2 IonQ launched a new quantum key distribution (QKD) product that sends multiple data types across existing municipal fiber networks. CEO: IonQ is the largest player in the QKD sector, with QKD network implementations in Europe and a QKD network in Korea; CFO: security is becoming part of nearly every customer discussion, IonQ now scans customer networks for quantum vulnerabilities, and security is 'our next growth vector'.

Space: IonQ now has 84 Skyloom optical communication terminals deployed on orbit, double the number a year ago; in Q2 it began work for the U.S. Space Development Agency on the HALO Europa contract, completing key design milestones toward delivering functioning satellites into orbit.
quarterly_data.figure: 84 Skyloom optical communication terminals on orbit

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: quantum-computing-as-a-service (QCaaS) revenue is growing even faster than organic computing revenue and is a very high margin business; IonQ sells full-stack (hardware, applications, QCaaS), and depending on the contract either IonQ or the customer owns application IP.

Customer EPB (Chattanooga): IonQ is opening a quantum memory R&D center close to customer EPB in Chattanooga; CEO: EPB now has an IonQ computer, a network and now memory (Lightsynq quantum-memory technology), and does energy grid optimization work with IonQ. CFO: quantum memory modules may also be sold to other quantum computer builders as part of the merchant supplier strategy.

CEO: IonQ is probably about half, if not the majority, of the revenue of the whole public quantum sector, and probably the majority of its R&D spend; CFO: demand for computing continues to be 'en fuego'.
